subject: Nanotechnology
title: Self-Assembly in Nature
description: A 60-second lesson on Self-Assembly in Nature.

hook.text: A tobacco mosaic virus assembles itself from 2130 identical protein copies around RNA — perfection without a blueprint.

buildup.text: Lipid bilayers, ribosomes, and microtubules all self-assemble — biology runs on spontaneous organization.

discovery.text: Natural self-assembly encodes structure in the shape and chemistry of each component — the part is the plan.

twist.text: Biological self-assembly uses energy — ATP drives microtubule growth, making it dynamic, not just thermodynamic.

climax.text: Biomimetic nanotechnology copies these natural designs — virus-like particles for vaccines are self-assembled shells.

punchline.text: Biology solved self-assembly billions of years ago — nano borrows the playbook.

quiz.question: How does a tobacco mosaic virus assemble without instructions?
options: An enzyme manually places each protein into position
Each protein's shape and chemistry encode where it fits, enabling spontaneous assembly around RNA
The virus copies its structure from a host cell template
